summary: The session positions context graphs within the broader field of context engineering. While knowledge graphs fill gaps in what agents know and which tools they can use, context graphs additionally encode rules and policies—answering why an agent should take a given action, making agents decision-aware rather than merely knowledgeable. Three memory types are described: short-term memory captures conversation history; long-term memory stores generalized context about organizations, people, and things; reasoning memory encodes policies and rules that guide task execution. The technical foundation involves an AI agent receiving a user query, checking its knowledge source, and if insufficient, querying the graph database via tools such as text-to-Cypher to traverse the graph and return reliable content. Andreas then introduces a decision-making framework. It begins with framing: identifying the local context, including the causality that led to the current decision point, the objective, and the environment (ranging from trivial purchasing to life-critical medical decisions). Next, global context incorporates past precedent and both hard and soft business rules. These feed into risk-value analysis, where the agent assesses the cost of being wrong—whether a life is at stake or merely an inconvenience—and what value is being maximized or minimized. A key concept is reference class validation: before acting, the agent must determine which subgroup applies, illustrated by the drug example where drug X is correct 99% of the time but fatal for 1%, and statistical averages cannot identify which group a specific patient belongs to. The output of risk-value analysis is not a decision but a proposal of alternatives with pros and cons. This proposal is handed to a deciding agent that checks whether it has authority to act; if not, it escalates to another agent or a human in the loop. The final and most important step is writing the entire reasoning chain—what was considered, what was not—back into the graph alongside the decision and actions taken. This transforms every decision into precedent that future agents can reference, creating a self-learning system. Andreas notes the framework can be implemented in LangGraph or ADK but cautions that particulars are highly domain-specific.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context Graphs Motivation
sections.summary: Zaid welcomes the audience to the Neo4j context graph session, framing the challenge of using knowledge graphs to fill gaps in AI agent knowledge, tools, and content. Agents excel at language, reasoning, and creativity but lack the knowledge puzzle piece.

sections.title: Memory Types and Graph Fundamentals
sections.summary: Three memory types are introduced: short-term (conversation history), long-term (contextual knowledge about organizations, people, things), and reasoning memory (policies and rules for decision-making). Graphs, made of nodes and relationships, capture deep and complex data connections.

sections.title: Why Context Graphs and Memory Graph Architecture
sections.summary: Context graphs shift focus from what an agent can do to why it should act, capturing policies and rules. A memory graph visualization shows short-term memory in green and long-term reasoning structures. The foundation architecture uses text-to-Cypher to query graph databases when knowledge sources are insufficient.

sections.title: Transition to Decision-Making Framework
sections.summary: Andreas introduces the need for a decision-making framework, using the open-claw robot example and a Red Bull-ordering autonomous agent to illustrate how agents encounter unforeseen circumstances. Multi-agent scaling amplifies the problem, requiring a thoughtful, explicit framework.

sections.title: Decision Framework: Framing, Global Context, and Risk-Value Analysis
sections.summary: The framework begins with framing: causality, objective, and environment define local context. Global context adds past precedent and hard/soft business rules. Risk-value analysis follows, with reference class validation as a key step—illustrated by the drug prescription example where 99% correctness masks a 1% fatal outcome that statistical reasoning cannot detect.

sections.title: Risk-Value Analysis, Act or Escalate, and Reasoning Chain Persistence
sections.summary: Andreas completes the framework. Risk-value analysis must explicitly assess the cost of being wrong (life at stake vs. minor inconvenience) and what value is maximized or minimized. Its output is a proposal of alternatives with pros and cons, not a decision. A separate deciding agent checks authority—either acting, escalating to another agent or human in the loop, or deferring. The final and most important step writes the entire reasoning chain back into the graph as precedent. The full workflow diagram is shown, implementable in LangGraph or ADK, though particulars remain domain-specific.

limitations: Statistical averages cannot identify which reference class a specific case belongs to, making them unreliable for high-stakes decisions
